papers.title: Sensitive period for song learning outlasts parent-offspring cohesion in wild zebra finches
papers.abstract: Communication is central to social behaviour, with vocalisations playing a crucial role in many species. In some species, vocalisations are learned, with songbirds being key to understanding vocal learning. The Australian zebra finch (Taeniopygia castanotis) is the most studied model organism for vocal learning. In captivity, juveniles are typically housed with their father, where males learn their father song and females develop a preference for that song. In nature, however, the social structure of zebra finches is more dynamic across space and time. To identify the natural social conditions during song learning, we followed zebra finch families across their early life in the wild using automated radio-tracking. The distance between juveniles and their parents increased post-fledging and became similar to the distance between juveniles and unrelated adults by the second half of the song learning period. These findings indicate a highly dynamic social environment during the song learning period and suggest that juvenile males could learn from many tutors and that females may develop broader song preferences. Thus, studies based on one-tutor paradigms should be interpreted carefully with respect to functional implications and highlight that future vocal learning studies could better reflect the social conditions under which song develops.

papers.title: A mechanistic classification of GNAO1 mutations links Gβ γ sequestration to hyperkinetic disease and treatment response
papers.abstract: Go is the most prevalent G protein subunit in the brain and is critical for signal transduction through G protein-coupled receptors. Mutations in the gene encoding Go (GNAO1) cause a rare neurodevelopmental disorder with involuntary movements (NEDIM) and, in some patients, developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). Here, we integrate human genetic analysis with cellular assays to define mechanistic classes of GNAO1 mutations and in vivo approaches to evaluate therapeutic strategies. We grouped variants into two functional categories: those predicted to sequester G{beta}{gamma} and those with reduced Go expression and therefore increased G{beta}{gamma} signaling. Analysis of patient data revealed that mutations predicted to impair G{beta}{gamma} release are significantly associated with NEDIM. Using the GNAO1R209H/+ mouse as a model of NEDIM, we evaluated two small molecules: caffeine, a nonselective adenosine receptor antagonist, and gallein, a selective modulator of G{beta}{gamma}-effector interactions. Both compounds significantly reduced hyperlocomotion in the open field test. Whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology revealed sex- and cell type-specific hyperexcitability in spiny projection neurons within the dorsolateral striatum of GNAO1R209H/+ mice. Together, these findings implicate dysfunction of dorsolateral striatal pathways in GNAO1-related disorder and suggest that mechanistic understanding of disease variants can guide targeted therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: BRET-Based Ligand Binding at Recombinant and Endogenous Dopamine D2 Receptors
papers.abstract: Dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) regulates diverse biological processes and is an important therapeutic target, underscoring the need for robust methods to quantify ligand binding at this receptor. Bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET)-based ligand binding assays have emerged as a powerful platform for quantifying binding in living cells, but their application to D2R has been limited by the availability of suitable fluorescent tracers. Here, we developed three far-red fluorescent antagonists (CELT-240, CELT-383, and CELT-385) as BRET tracers for D2R. All three compounds produced specific, saturable D2R binding with nanomolar affinity. Further characterization of CELT-385 demonstrated its utility for kinetic and competition binding measurements and revealed high affinity binding at the closely related dopamine D3 receptor (D3R). We also extended BRET-based ligand binding beyond genetically-modified receptors using bystander BRET, enabling measurements at unmodified recombinant and endogenously expressed D2R. Together, these findings provide new tools for quantitative D2R/D3R ligand binding and a template for extending BRET-based ligand binding to endogenously expressed GPCRs.

papers.title: In vivo optical induction of INaL by photoactivation of AaH-II peptide in beating heart using wireless implantable device
papers.abstract: Precise spatiotemporal control of pharmacological compounds in cardiac tissue remains an unmet challenge. Systemic drug administration poorly reproduces the localized and transient nature of cardiac events. Photopharmacology, in which light controls drug activity, offers a compelling solution, but its translation to the beating heart requires wireless light delivery to a moving, soft, and electrically active organ. Here, we demonstrate the first in vivo use of a wireless device to photoactivate a peptide that modulates cardiac excitability. Using a flexible, battery-free implantable optoelectronic device, we achieved light-triggered uncaging of AaH-II*, a natural peptide that enhances the late sodium current. We first validated the caged peptide in vitro and ex vivo, showing that caging suppresses its activity and that UV illumination rapidly restores it. In vivo, wireless photoactivation produced a clear modulation of cardiac electrical activity, as monitored by electrocardiography. This work establishes device-based peptide photomodulation as a strategy for remote, temporally controlled pharmacological intervention in the heart. More broadly, it provides a new platform for probing cardiac excitability and developing region-targeted therapies.

papers.title: Preprint solicitation as a natural experiment in scholarly publishing
papers.abstract: Preprinting is a growing and increasingly recognized mechanism for scientific communication and productivity and a way to facilitate global access to science. The interplay of preprinting practices with formal peer-reviewed publication is an open question that is now tractable to targeted analysis. Here, we take advantage of nearly a decade of preprint solicitation at Proceedings B to address this question, which offers a quasi-experimental setting for comparing outcomes for solicited preprints and traditionally submitted manuscripts. We used submission records from 15,368 manuscripts from 2018-2024 to assess whether preprint solicitation affects acceptance rates, journal scope, author geographic diversity, and post-publication uptake. Solicited manuscripts were accepted at nearly twice the rate of traditional submissions and received more downloads and citations after publication. Submission topics were broadly similar between the two routes, though solicited manuscripts showed marginally greater subject diversity. Geographic disparities favoring the Global North persisted, but acceptance rates for solicited manuscripts converged across regions, narrowing the gap seen in traditional submissions. These findings extend earlier work on this initiative and indicate that editor-driven solicitation can identify high-quality preprints, broaden geographic representation, and increase research visibility, offering a replicable model for journals seeking to diversify authorship while maintaining editorial standards.

papers.title: Screening and evaluation of medicine food homology herbal combinations for ameliorating chemotherapy induced ovarian aging under an integrated multi-strategy framework
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Ovarian aging poses a serious threat to women's reproductive health. Medicine food homology (MFH) herbs, owing to their favorable safety profile and suitability for long-term use, have become important interventional resources. However, conventional formula screening relies largely on empirical statistics and lacks mechanistic evidence and a systematic screening strategy. Methods: In this study, we integrated single cell transcriptomic analysis, human use evidence mining, UPLC/Q TOF MS chemical profiling and pretrained protein molecular representation models to establish a multi strategy framework for the discovery of MFH herbal combinations. Single cell transcriptomic datasets related to ovarian aging from the GEO database were analyzed to identify key pathological processes and candidate targets. High-frequency MFH herbs were selected by mining classical prescriptions and clinical literature. By comparing six protein molecular pretrained representation combinations, ESM T5 was identified for compound target affinity prediction and validated by molecular dynamics simulation and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) assays, ultimately identifying the Astragalus ginseng (Huangqi Renshen) herb pair (HXF) as the core candidate. Functional expression validation of key targets was performed, and the efficacy of HXF and the expression of related molecules were verified in a D gal induced KGN granulosa cell senescence model and a cyclophosphamide-induced rat model of diminished ovarian function. Results: Single cell analysis revealed that ovarian aging was characterized by impaired steroidogenesis, enhanced MDK NCL communication between granulosa cells and immune cells, and extracellular matrix remodeling, with CYP19A1, SERPINE1 and MDK as key targets. By further integrating human-use evidence mining and UPLC/Q TOF MS compound annotation, an MFH compound library comprising 712 molecules was established. ESM T5 prediction, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and SPR assays confirmed that multiple constituents of Astragalus and ginseng exhibited favorable binding activity toward key targets. At the cellular level, knockdown of MDK or SERPINE1 attenuated the senescence phenotype, whereas knockdown of CYP19A1 aggravated it. In vitro and in vivo experiments demonstrated that Astragalus ginseng ameliorated granulosa cell senescence and diminished ovarian function in rats, restored CYP19A1 related steroidogenesis, downregulated inflammation- and matrix remodeling related molecules such as SERPINE1 and IL18, and reduced MDK NCL colocalization signals. Conclusion: This study established a multi-strategy screening framework integrating disease mechanism decoding, human use evidence constraints and pretrained model prediction, and identified Astragalus ginseng as a candidate herb pair for ameliorating ovarian aging. Its effects may be associated with promoting steroidogenesis, suppressing SERPINE1/IL18 related inflammation and matrix remodeling, and modulating MDK NCL signaling. These findings provide a strategic reference for the mechanism oriented discovery of MFH herbal combinations.

papers.title: What do navigating animals see? Reconstructing the visual histories of desert ants
papers.abstract: To understand how brains translate sensory input into behavioural outputs requires a fuller account of the sensory experience of individual animals in their natural settings. Previously we developed a visual rendering software capable of reconstructing the information that insect's compound eyes perceive (Millward et al, 2022). In this work, we extend this software pipeline to integrate data from animal tracking, habitat mapping, and compound eye modelling methods. The result is a new type of dataset that documents the natural foraging behaviour of desert ants (a model species for the study of animal navigation) within their natural habitat, combined with simulation tools to accurately reconstruct the visual experience of each forager as they learned to navigate their surroundings. This addresses a long-held need to create realistic training input for brain models complimented with verification tests in the same real ecologically relevant scenarios.

papers.title: Modulation of planarian seizure-like activity via antiseizure medications
papers.abstract: Acute chemical exposure to organophosphorus compounds (OPs) arising from terrorist attacks or accidental poisonings pose a serious threat to human health. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition due to acute OP exposure causes a cholinergic crisis, manifested as increased secretions, respiratory distress, loss of consciousness, seizures, and ultimately death if left untreated. Benzodiazepines, such as midazolam, are currently used to stop OP-induced seizures, but must be administered within minutes after exposure to be effective. This makes midazolam impractical for large-scale civilian emergencies. Thus, there is a need to identify novel antiseizure medications (ASMs) that are equally effective even when administered later. It has been challenging to identify such compounds with traditional mammalian testing; high throughput screening assays that can quickly and cost-effectively evaluate many candidates for their potential as an ASM are needed. Planarians are aquatic invertebrates that are suitable organismal models for OP neurotoxicity studies due to the conservation of OP targets and their ability to metabolize OPs. Here, we built on our prior work that introduced a computational image analysis pipeline to quantify planarian seizure-like activity (pSLA) in two planarian species (Dugesia japonica and Girardia dorotocephala). We previously used this approach to characterize pSLA following acute exposure (up to 30 minutes) to seizurogenic compounds. In the present study, we asked whether pSLA induced by the OP pesticide parathion, pentylenetetrazole, or NMDA could be rescued by co-exposure to four ASMs: midazolam, topiramate, MK-801, and carbamazepine. All tested ASMs were effective at reducing parathion-induced pSLA in one planarian species. However, ASM responses varied substantially across proconvulsants and planarian species. Defining the molecular mechanisms underlying pSLA will be essential for establishing planarians as a reliable model for ASM discovery.

papers.title: Fine-tuning an intracellular allosteric pocket programs GPCR signaling bias
papers.abstract: Biased signaling of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) offers a route for precise therapeutics with fewer adverse effects. Intracellular allosteric ligands can impose such bias, yet how subtle chemical changes within these pockets reshape receptor-transducer coupling and downstream signaling remains unclear. Here, we systematically fine-tuned the intracellular allosteric pocket of neurotensin receptor 1 (NTSR1) through chemical modification of the {beta}-arrestin-biased ligand SBI-553. Minor changes to the ligand scaffold altered transducer-coupling preferences, generating distinct profiles of G-protein and {beta}-arrestin signaling. Cryo-electron microscopy structures of NTSR1-{beta}-arrestin2 complexes bound to designed allosteric probes revealed ligand-dependent remodeling of the intracellular cavity that reshapes the receptor-effector interface. Alanine scanning identified transducer-sensitive residues within and beyond the immediate ligand-contact region. In mice, SBI-553 and N065 produced distinct physiological profiles, with N065 improving survival in a lethal endotoxemia model. Finally, phosphoproteomic profiling revealed partially overlapping but distinct downstream signaling profiles among the three modulators. Together, these findings establish the intracellular allosteric pocket as a tunable determinant of transducer coupling and show that closely related modulators can generate distinct signaling and physiological profiles.

papers.title: Striatal M4 Receptors Mediate M4 PAM Antipsychotic-like Efficacy Independently of Normalizing Striatal Dopamine Release
papers.abstract: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor (mAChR) drugs have emerged as a promising new class of antipsychotics, highlighted by the FDA approval of Cobenfy, the first treatment for schizophrenia that does not directly target dopamine receptors. The M4 receptor subtype is thought to be a key mediator of antipsychotic-like efficacy. However, the in vivo circuit mechanisms underlying the antipsychotic-like efficacy observed with M4-selective positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) remain incompletely understood. Here, we used fiber photometry in awake, behaving mice to assess how the M4 PAM VU0467154 (VU'154) affects striatal dopamine (DA) transmission under basal and amphetamine-stimulated conditions. We also generated and validated dorsal striatum-specific M4 knockout mice (DS-M4-KO) to test the role of striatal M4 receptors in regulating DA release and antipsychotic-like effects. VU'154 dose-dependently reduced the amplitude of striatal DA release events under basal conditions without altering event frequency. However, VU'154 had no significant effects on tonic DA levels under basal conditions, as assessed using the D1 PAM DETQ. Despite robustly attenuating AHL, VU'154 produced little to no effect on amphetamine-induced DA levels, indicating that antipsychotic-like efficacy was dissociated from changes in striatal DA levels. Notably, VU'154 efficacy in AHL was absent in DS-M4-KO mice, demonstrating that M4 receptors in the dorsal striatum are required for antipsychotic-like effects. Combined with previous studies implicating a key role for M4 receptors on D1-expressing neurons, these findings suggest that M4 PAMs produce antipsychotic-like efficacy primarily through postsynaptic mechanisms in the dorsal striatum, rather than through broad normalization of amphetamine-induced DA release.

papers.title: Movements for Grooming in Rhesus Macaques Co-opted from Feeding Movements
papers.abstract: Abstract Catarrhine primates exhibit a wide range of skilled hand movements, including those used for foraging and grooming, and their evolution attracts ongoing attention. Competing hypotheses are that skilled hand movements evolved for feeding, or that the hand movements of various behaviors evolved independently. The present study addressed these questions by asking whether the movements of grooming of rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) are co-opted from feeding movements. We video-recorded free-ranging rhesus macaques in the Cayo Santiago colony of the Caribbean Primate Research Center (CPRC), University of Puerto Rico. Allogrooming (grooming a conspecific), self-grooming, and rhythmic scratching with a hand or foot were compared with a common foraging behavior, geophagy, mining and eating soil. Allogrooming, self-grooming, and foraging occurred in visually mediated bouts that featured numerous comb and brush hand movements directed toward searching for a target in the fur or soil. Once located, the target was grasped between the thumb and index finger in a pincer grip to be placed in the mouth - or less often bitted or licked from the fur. Hand movements were generally directed toward the actor but were also influenced by object-surface features, including fur direction during grooming and the rocks and debris covering soil targets during geophagy. The grooming movements of comb, brush, and grasp were recognizably those used during foraging. Rhythmic scratching with a hand or foot was not visually guided but did employ a comb movement of the digits of the hand or foot. Thus, with the exception of the rhythmicity of scratching, the hand movements of grooming are fundamentally foraging movements. It is proposed that grooming movements are coopted from oromanual feeding movements in macaques, a relationship that may be widespread in other species.

papers.title: Characterization of the Preclinical in Vitro and in Vivo Pharmacokinetic Properties of the Cyclic Oligomeric Depsipeptide Ryanodine Receptor 2 Inhibitor ent-Verticilide
papers.abstract: ent-Verticilide is a synthetic cyclic oligomeric depsipeptide that inhibits ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2)-mediated calcium (Ca) leak and has demonstrated antiarrhythmic activity in mice. This study characterized the preclinical absorption, distribution, metabolism, and pharmacokinetic properties of ent-verticilide and investigated factors affecting its oral exposure. ent-Verticilide was stable in rat plasma and simulated gastric and intestinal fluids but exhibited extensive plasma protein binding (>94%) and low apparent permeability in Caco-2 cells, with no evidence of pronounced net efflux. In rat and human liver microsomes, ent-verticilide underwent rapid NADPH-dependent metabolism, with an in vitro half-life of 5.43 min and 4.35 min, respectively, and a predicted hepatic extraction ratio of 0.90 and 0.92, respectively. Following intravenous administration in rats, ent-verticilide exhibited a systemic clearance of 25.5 mL/min/kg and a large steady-state volume of distribution (4.72 L/kg). Absolute oral bioavailability was approximately 16%. Simultaneous portal and systemic sampling estimated intestinal availability (FaFg) at 0.25 and hepatic availability (Fh) at 0.64, suggesting that processes occurring before hepatic entry are a major limitation to oral exposure. Pretreatment with the CYP inhibitor 1-aminobenzotriazole increased portal and systemic exposure approximately 10.6- and 18.5-fold, respectively, and increased apparent Fh to approximately 1. Collectively, these findings identify limited intestinal availability and CYP-mediated presystemic metabolism as important determinants of ent-verticilide exposure and provide a framework for its continued development as an RyR2-targeted therapeutic.

papers.title: A step beyond: age and sex-dependent changes in multidimensional locomotor and gait patterns of voluntary motion of C57BL/6 mice
papers.abstract: Age-related decreases in physical activity drive frailty and reduced intrinsic capacity, promoting adverse health outcomes such as falls. Experimental tools for quantifying these metrics in preclinical models have lagged behind those used clinically; single-endpoint activity assessments (e.g., rotarod performance, treadmill activity) of rodents often require invasive handling and/or forced performance cues that may increase stress and variability, especially in aged animals. Here, we evaluated whether automated analysis of spontaneous movement using machine-learning-based software (Palmreader) could identify age-related changes in locomotor activity, gait, paw loading, or posture in male and female C57BL/6 mice across young, adult, and aged timepoints (4.5-, 7-, and 22 months of age). Parameters were quantified using the BlackBox One system during a 7-minute open-field recording. Principal component analysis demonstrated age-related separation of movement phenotypes, with individual parameters demonstrating increased hindlimb duty factor and longer stride lengths with age. Age-related changes in forelimb-to-hindlimb duty-factor imbalance, paw contact, and postural organization were also observed, and several gait alterations with age showed different patterns between males and females. Conventional measures of physical activity (e.g., distance traveled, walking time), in contrast, showed few age-related differences, particularly in females. These findings suggest that aging more consistently alters movement patterns rather than movement magnitude, and that gait and postural features may represent important age-related functional changes not captured by activity measurements alone. Automated assessment of spontaneous movement may therefore represent a useful complement to traditional physical activity testing, with the added benefit of minimal animal handling and short recording times.

papers.title: Figuring things out: Innovation arena in wolves and dogs
papers.abstract: Dogs and wolves present an interesting lens through which to examine innovative behaviors, as both of their environments promote the development of innovations for different reasons. Dogs' natural environment (as free-ranging animals) is characterized by high diversity and abundance in novel feeding opportunities. Conversely, wolves live in an unpredictable and harsh environment in which adapting to sudden scarcity is vital for survival. Thus, to analyze the role of the environment in innovative behavior (both evolutionarily and ontogenetically) we studied problem-solving skills of three populations: captive wolves, "pack dogs" (raised similarly to the wolves), and pet dogs. For this, we used an "innovation arena" (after Rossler & Mioduszewska et al., 2020) consisting of 9 novel puzzle boxes presented simultaneously. Pet dogs were better at solving the boxes than their pack-living counterparts, which could point towards prior positive experiences with similar opportunities (here, human-created constructs) providing motivation to interact with novel features of the environment, which would eventually lead to innovation. We found little effect of evolution: wolves needed more time to approach the boxes (potentially due to neophobia), but both wolves and pack dogs interacted with and solved the boxes to a similar extent.

papers.title: Ambient light color does not detectably change the transient, flight-specific DEET response of Aedes aegypti
papers.abstract: We asked whether ambient light color changes how Aedes aegypti respond to the repellent DEET. We reanalyzed an unpublished image dataset from the chamber system of Carver (2018): 12 recordings of about 20 mosquitoes each, under six light colors (blue, green, orange, red, white, yellow), with one recording per color in each of two sessions. Each recording had about 10 minutes with bait only and then about 10 minutes with bait plus DEET. We report two robust findings and one negative result. First, the DEET response is short-lived. Pooled across all 12 recordings, flight motion fell by about half in the minute of DEET onset and recovered within about three minutes (ratio of means 1.99, exact sign-flip one-sided p=0.058); over the full halves there was no net difference (ratio of means 1.01, p=0.49). Second, the drop is a loss of flight, not a loss of detection. A separate presence readout, which also counts resting mosquitoes, stayed almost flat (5.6 to 5.1 detections per frame) while flight fell from 0.51 to 0.35 events per frame pair. The chamber is closed, so presence by itself is not a finding; it shows that the animals remained detectable while flight collapsed, and the recovery of flight excludes mortality. Third, we could not show that color changes the response. A detectability control ruled out an imaging artifact. A baseline-activity control then showed that the apparent color ranking follows how much the mosquitoes flew before DEET (Spearman +0.83). Under a null with no color effect, 1.5 of 6 colors pass the cross-session concordance bar by chance. After adjusting for baseline activity and for selection among six colors, no color stood out (p=0.47). Ratio-of-halves suppression measures in chamber assays are confounded with baseline activity, and prospective studies should match activity across conditions or use time-matched within-recording contrasts.

papers.title: Individual-level social associations and social information use predict foraging success in winter mixed-species flocks
papers.abstract: The acquisition of social information to improve foraging efficiency is considered one of the primary drivers of mixed-species flocks (MSFs). This flow of social information occurs among individuals of multiple species, but analyses of MSFs at the level of species fail to capture the nuances of this dynamic. We investigated how individual-level social associations in North American MSFs impact discovery of novel feeders presented alongside vocal cues. We used radio-frequency identification (RFID) data loggers to track arrivals of individually tagged black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus), white-breasted nuthatches (Sitta carolinensis), and downy woodpeckers (Dryobates pubescens) at fixed feeders, and during novel feeder trials paired with chickadee, nuthatch, or white noise playbacks. For chickadees, a higher number of total associations and conspecific playbacks improved novel feeder discovery. The foraging benefits in nuthatches and woodpeckers were predicted by their individual-level associations with chickadees and these benefits only manifested during chickadee playbacks. We demonstrate that the advantages of mixed-species flocking are not uniformly distributed across species; rather, they are contingent upon individually maintained social associations and the presence of social information. These findings highlight the necessity of quantifying individual variation to accurately assess the evolutionary drivers and fitness consequences of species interactions.

papers.title: Data-driven frame-by-frame analysis of surface swimming and terrestrial walking in the coastal beetle Phaleria atriceps
papers.abstract: Background. Inter-leg coordination of insects changes depending on environmental conditions. Although locomotor changes between terrestrial and aquatic environments have been examined in various insects, relatively little is known about coastal insects living at the boundary between these environments. We therefore compared the inter-leg coordination during terrestrial walking with that during surface swimming in the coastal beetle Phaleria atriceps. Methods. Surface swimming was recorded in 17 individuals and terrestrial walking in 10 individuals using high-speed video at 1,000 frames/s. The six leg tips and anterior and posterior body landmarks were tracked frame-by-frame using DeepLabCut, and leg movements were quantified in a body-centered coordinate system. Leg movement periods were estimated from sinusoidal fits to longitudinal leg-tip trajectories. Inter-leg phase relationships were calculated for all 15 leg pairs and integrated to reconstruct a representative six-leg phase organization for each locomotor mode. Results. Leg movement periods were significantly longer during surface swimming than during terrestrial walking for all six legs. During walking, the six-leg phase relationship closely matched an alternating tripod pattern, with a left foreleg (L1), a right middle leg (R2), and a left hind leg (L3) forming one phase group and a right foreleg (R1), a left middle leg (L2), and a right hind leg (R3) forming the opposing group. The same broad grouping was observed in the six-leg phase relationship during surface swimming, although significant differences in relative phase were detected for L1-L2, L1-R2, and R1-R2. Conclusions. Phaleria atriceps exhibited six-leg phase relationships broadly consistent with an alternating tripod pattern during both terrestrial walking and surface swimming, whereas leg movement periods and certain inter-leg phase relationships differed between the two locomotor modes. These findings provide a quantitative description of the similarities and differences in inter-leg coordination between terrestrial walking and surface swimming in a coastal beetle. Further mechanical and comparative studies will be needed to clarify the functional and evolutionary significance of these findings.

papers.title: Studies on a luminescent antimicrobial metal complex reveal a method to directly image pathogenic bacterial infection in a living organism using optical microscopy
papers.abstract: Methods to render Galleria Mellonella larvae transparent allowing three-dimensional viewing of larvae through orthodox light microscopy techniques are reported. To explore this models capability, we exploited the imaging properties of a metal complex antimicrobial to probe its therapeutic action against a pathogenic Acetinobacter baumannii infection. To illustrate the general utility of this method, we have also used the commercial fluorescent dye, Alexafluor-488, to image bacteria within live larvae.

papers.title: Stabilizing the CHI3L1-Gal3BP complex remodels the glioblastoma immune microenvironment and synergizes with PD-1 blockade
papers.abstract: CHI3L1 (YKL-40) is associated with mesenchymal, treatment-resistant glioblastoma (GBM) and shapes macrophage programs through interactions with galectin-3 or galectin-3-binding protein (Gal3BP). However, the CHI3L1-Gal3BP interaction has not been previously targeted. A surface plasmon resonance screen identified LZ6. Ternary complex formation was assessed by fluorescence-based, biophysical, and mass spectrometry methods. Activity was evaluated in five patient-derived GBM lines, myeloid cultures from eight donors, CRISPR interference with guide-resistant rescue, and a four-arm factorial study of orthotopic GL261 tumors. LZ6 increased Gal3BP engagement 3.4-fold while reducing galectin-3 in vitro. In GBM-conditioned cultures, LZ6 raised phagocytosis 22% to 44% and MHC class II 24% to 39% and lowered CD206 45% to 31% and IL-10 105 to 67 pg/mL, with concordant transcripts. Gal3BP knockdown reduced the response 41%; guide-resistant rescue restored it. Oral LZ6 raised the intratumoral Gal3BP:galectin-3 ratio from 1.02 to 1.56 at unchanged CHI3L1. In tumor tissue LZ6 shifted 20 of 24 immune endpoints, lowering CD206 and IL-10 and raising MHC class II and CD8 effector function. Median survival with LZ6 was 52.4 versus 26.3 days (P = 0.0012), and in combination with anti-PD-1 most animals survived to the end of follow-up (median not reached), with a significant factorial interaction (hazard ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.10-0.57, P = 0.0014). LZ6 is a molecular glue of the CHI3L1-Gal3BP complex that engages its target in brain tumor after oral dosing and extends survival alone and synergistically with PD-1 blockade.

papers.title: End-to-end automation of behavioural experiments with a collaborative robot
papers.abstract: Reliable behavioural measurement is critical to neuroscience discovery, but end-to-end automation of experiments using live animals is challenging. Preparation and transfer of live animals into and out of behavioural assays require skilled, dexterous, gentle and consistent handling. This is difficult to achieve without bespoke automation systems, which resist wide adoption. We present STELA, a robotic cell featuring off-the-shelf collaborative robot (cobot) that autonomously runs the complete workflow of a Drosophila behaviour experiment, from vial to data. Designed to emulate human routine fly laboratory procedures in human workspace, it performs manipulation of fly culture vials, CO2 fly anaesthesia, vision-guided sex classification, single live fly manipulation, and loading and disassembly of a behaviour assay, all in a programmed loop. In 24-h working day, STELA completed 16 experiments (1024 individual visual learning assays in flies) compared to the human who, in an 8-hour working day, completed 6 (384 assays). Retention of flies fit for analysis was similar (93.85% versus 83.33%, respectively), but with 12-fold improvement in handling consistency by the robot. In biologically matched behaviour experiments, robotic and manual handling resulted in the same mean fly behavioural outcomes, yet the robot significantly reduced inter-individual variability in baseline and learning behaviours. STELA demonstrates that it is possible to deploy standard robotic systems to flexibly automate one of the most challenging animal experiments. It provides a low-variance, high-throughput platform for scalable experimentation, and a path to closed-loop, democratized robotic acceleration of experimental discovery.

papers.title: Bio-Templated Zinc Oxide Nanotherapeutics from Flemingia macrophylla kuntze Ex Merr: In Vivo Anti-Diabetic and Anti-Inflammatory Efficacy in Drosophila melanogaster
papers.abstract: Nanotechnology has a major impact on the creation of novel and effective therapies for the treatment of several diseases, including diabetes and cancer. The current work is a report on the use of the aqueous extract from the leaves of the Flemingia macrophylla plant as a capping and reducing agent in the green synthesis of zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO-NPs).The synthesized ZnO-NPs were subjected to characterization through X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy (UV-Vis). Dose-dependent in vivo effects were investigated using Drosophila melanogaster subjected to a high-sugar diet (HSD) to induce a diabetic-like model. In vitro anti-oxidant, anti-diabetic, anti-inflammatory assay, survival, locomotor function, neuroanatomical integrity, ovary and testis morphology, egg-laying capacity, and male fertility were evaluated. The most prominent UV-visible peak was detected at around 370 nm. Structural and morphological analysis via XRD and electron microscopy confirmed the hexagonal phase of the ZnO-NPs, indicating an average calcined particle size of around 47 nm at 500 degree C. The manuscript reports significant anti-diabetic and anti-inflammatory effects in vitro and in the in vivo Drosophila model, together with antioxidant activity. The in vivo results indicate that green-synthesized ZnO-NPs mitigate adverse phenotypes triggered by a high-sugar diet and also potential as an anti-diabetic intervention and warrant further mechanistic and preclinical investigation. Keywords: Flemingia macrophylla; Green ZnO-NPs; Drosophila melanogaster; high-sugar diet; nanobiotechnology

papers.title: Bayesian Stacking of Quantitative Adverse Outcome Pathways Isolates Primary Drivers of Liver Steatosis
papers.abstract: The quantification of adverse outcome pathways (qAOPs) involving multiple converging pathways remains a fundamental challenge in toxicology. This difficulty is worsened by small in vitro datasets with missing values and heteroscedasticity, which limit the estimation of non-linear response functions and the robust estimation of uncertainty. To overcome these limitations, we developed a framework for estimating a Bayesian qAOP Ensemble (Bayesian qAOPE) that combines heteroscedastic dose-response functions with continuous splines and linear models. By combining multiple converging non-linear pathways through Bayesian stacking, the most meaningful pathways are identified, and strongly correlated responses are naturally accounted for. Applying our approach to a hepatic steatosis dataset, we demonstrate by exact Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation that our framework yields an exceptional predictive performance suitable for the derivation of a probabilistically weighted Benchmark Dose (BMD). Our framework is highly adaptable and provides a chemical-agnostic, mathematically founded blueprint for integrating multiple converging pathways in a Bayesian network.

papers.title: Primary Human Macrophages Exhibit Functional CYP3A4 Activity with Marked Expression-Function Discordance and Cocaine-Induced Catalytic Activation
papers.abstract: CYP3A4 is a phase I drug-metabolizing enzyme responsible for transformation of ~50% of clinically relevant drugs. While extensively characterized in hepatocytes, its role in immune cells remains poorly understood. Here, using primary human monocyte-derived macrophages, we identify an understudied extrahepatic site of CYP3A4-mediated drug metabolism. Macrophages from 100 independent donors expressed CYP3A4 and its transcriptional regulators, Pregnane X Receptor (PXR) and Constitutive Androstane Receptor (CAR), with substantial interindividual variability. Importantly, CYP3A4 protein expression was accompanied by measurable catalytic activity in intact macrophages, yet CYP3A4 mRNA, protein abundance, and activity lacked concordance, demonstrating that expression alone may not predict function. In vivo, CYP3A4 was expressed in rhesus macaque Kupffer cells, further supporting macrophages as a potential pharmacologic entity. We next evaluated cocaine as a potential modulator of CYP3A4, due to its role in xenobiotic clearance. Cocaine had a dichotomous effect on expression, increasing CYP3A4 in some donors while producing no change or decreases in others, a phenotype associated with PXR, CAR, and the sigma-1 cocaine receptor. Strikingly, despite these divergent expression responses, cocaine increased CYP3A4 catalytic activity in all donors, reaching or exceeding levels induced by rifampicin, a clinically relevant CYP3A4 inducer. In rhesus macaques, cocaine also decreased antiretroviral therapy tissue concentrations, coincident with increased CYP3A4 and PXR. Together, these findings establish macrophages as a functionally active extrahepatic site of CYP3A4 metabolism and reveal a critical disconnect between CYP3A4 expression and catalytic function. Moreover, our findings identify interindividual variability and expression-activity discordance as important considerations for personalized medicine and understanding clinically relevant drug-drug interactions in the context of substance use.

papers.title: Human CYP1A2 metabolism of organophosphorus pesticides and nerve agent surrogates
papers.abstract: CYP1A2 contributes 13-15% of hepatic CYP450 content and plays a critical role in the metabolism of approximately 10% of pharmaceutical drugs in the human body. CYP1A2 has been previously reported to bioactivate and detoxify both the thion (P=S) and oxon (P=O) forms of organophosphorus (OP) compounds. In this study, we determined the capacity of CYP1A2 to degrade OP compounds using LC-MS/MS, as well as the inhibition of its activity by OP compounds using the previously developed pFluor50 assay. CYP1A2 was selective in metabolizing thions over oxons, and several OP compounds inhibited its activity in a time- and dose-dependent manner. To further investigate the mechanism of CYP1A2-OP interactions, molecular docking studies were performed using a crystal structure of CYP1A2 (PDB ID: 2HI4). Linear correlation analysis between CYP1A2 inhibition at 10 M with 30 minute preincubation and the % OP compound remaining at 2 hours (R = -0.71, P<0.001) showed a moderate but significant correlation. Based on these findings, CYP1A2 was identified as a potential bioscavenger for OP compound metabolism, supporting the future integration of experimental and in silico data for developing artificial intelligence (AI) / machine learning (ML) models for prediction of CYP1A2-mediated metabolism of existing and emerging OP compounds, including those of toxicological and chemical warfare relevance.

papers.title: Camus: a video-based framework for continuous behavioral monitoring in the mouse home-cage
papers.abstract: Home-cage activity is a window into the spontaneous behavioral repertoire of mice. These behaviors are organized across the circadian cycle, and disruptions in their duration, frequency, or organization may provide sensitive measures of neurological or psychiatric dysfunction. While continuous monitoring can help track the dynamics of spontaneous behavior, video recording in conventional laboratory cages is limited by compact cage geometry, opaque cage tops, and obstructed views of animals, food, and water. We therefore developed Camus, a Camera for home-cage recordings of Mus musculus mice. Camus integrates off-the-shelf USB cameras with infrared illumination and custom 3D-printed components for access to food and water without obstructed views. The modular design pairs continuous video acquisition with a manually validated computer-vision model to quantify locomotion, feeding, drinking, and nesting-related behavior across multiday recordings. A single desktop computer can record as many as 20 cages in parallel at an incremental cost of approximately $250 per cage, recording more than 99% of expected frames at 640x360-pixel resolution and 30 frames per second. Camus captured circadian structure in locomotion, feeding, and drinking. Camus also captured nest-building and sex-specific differences in nest dynamics. Using Camus with transgenic 5xFAD mice overexpressing amyloid revealed selective, age-progressive deficits in nesting behavior. Camus provides a scalable, open-source platform that combines accessible hardware, automated video monitoring, and machine-learning based analysis for continuous and potentially longitudinal behavioral phenotyping.

papers.title: Assessing larger-than rule learning in African grey parrots (Psittacus erithacus).
papers.abstract: Many animals discriminate between magnitudes (e.g., in size, quantity, volume, length) that have fitness implications. Accumulated experience may facilitate the formation of relational rules that can be applied in novel contexts. However, the extent to which animals can form a relational rule, and are able to apply it to novel contexts remains a core focus when understanding the evolution of cognition. Here, we assessed the ability of African grey parrots o acquire the relative larger-than rule in size or quantity discrimination, and if so, how this was learned. Eight captive parrots initially participated in a natural preference test (NPT) to assess their prior preference for a larger amount of seeds. Each parrot was then randomly selected to either acquire the larger-than rule in size or quantity in a basic training (BT). They then participated in transfer training (TT) to evaluate their ability to apply the learned rule to novel stimulus pairs, and a final transfer test (FTT) to assess whether the parrots could generalise the learned rule to unseen stimulus pairs beyond the training range. Six parrots successfully completed both training and the test, with only one parrot, Sensei, passing the quantity discrimination FTT. More detailed analyses showed that the parrots showed varied performance in the TT, but as a group, showed limited transfer in the TT, suggesting the use of associative learning through increased experience in BT. They also showed better performance if a stimulus pair had a larger difference (Webers law). The success of Sensei was attributed to extensive TT alongside his quick natural preference toward larger amounts. These results suggest that repeated exposure to TT stimulus pairs increases familiarity with the stimulus pairs, which can facilitate task success, but individuals vary in their ability to acquire relational rules.

papers.title: Same-sex sexual behaviour reduces reproductive success but mitigates aggression in a subsocial insect
papers.abstract: Same-sex sexual behaviour (SSB) is widely observed across taxa, yet its evolutionary maintenance remains debated and its fitness consequences remain surprisingly understudied. Here, we quantified the fitness consequences of male SSB in the burying beetle Nicrophorus vespilloides and tested three prominent hypotheses about its function: (i) that it provides practice for future mating, (ii) that it reduces tension through dominance assertion, and (iii) that it arises indirectly from indiscriminate mating. Males were observed in same-sex pairings to quantify SSB and then paired with females to measure their subsequent mating behaviour and reproductive success. Same-sex sexual behaviour was common, occurring in 55% of same-sex pairs, and was associated with reduced reproductive success driven by higher brood failure rates. Both males that initiated, and those that received, mounting attempts from other males suffered reduced fitness. Contrary to the practice hypothesis, SSB did not increase mating speed with females and was associated with reduced mating frequency. However, SSB was associated with reduced aggression, supporting the hypothesis that SSB reduces tension through dominance establishment. Our findings show that SSB can reduce reproductive success but may be maintained due to a beneficial reduction in aggression.

papers.title: COGNITIVE HETEROGENEITY AND AGING: AN AGE-INDEPENDENT CILIARY GENE PROGRAM TRACKS COGNITIVE RESILIENCE IN MICE
papers.abstract: Cognitive decline with age is often viewed as inevitable, yet older animals show striking heterogeneity in functional trajectories, with many preserving cognitive integrity despite physiological decline. The biological basis of this resilience remains poorly understood, partly due to insensitive behavioral testing paradigms. Using an automated home-cage platform and hippocampal RNA sequencing, we integrated behavioral phenotyping with transcriptomic profiling to disentangle molecular programs linked to cognitive performance from chronological age. Behavioral data from 906 C57BL/6 mice across 129 standardized studies, trajectory-based modeling, variance-partitioned correlation, and stability-driven gene prioritization identified a transcriptional signature (271 genes) linked to cognitive state independent of age. Preserved cognition was associated with higher expression of genes governing ciliary structure and motility, neurite organization, and synaptic architecture, while impairment was associated with neuroimmune and metabolic-stress programs. A 38-gene cilia structural module score remained associated with resilience after controlling for age (partial rho = -0.81), with consistent effects across leave-one-out resampling. Because the constituent genes were selected on this same outcome, the module-level magnitude is not an unbiased effect-size estimate; recalibration against a null that reapplies the full selection procedure gave an empirical p of 0.026. This divergence emerged among genetically identical mice, indicating non-genetic, discrete hippocampal molecular signatures underlying individual differences. Cell-type attribution against the Allen Brain Cell Atlas localized the module predominantly to ependymal cells, with 27 of 38 genes ependymal-restricted (median detection 90.2% in ependymal cells versus 1.1% in CA1 glutamatergic neurons) and three genes (Dnah9, Dnai4, Kif9) also detected in CA1. The association was not attributable to ependymal tissue content: the module score was unrelated to Foxj1 expression (rho = -0.016) and the partial correlation was unchanged after adjustment for ependymal and choroid plexus marker panels, indicating that the module reflects how strongly the ciliary program is expressed rather than how many ependymal cells each sample contained. These findings support a conceptual shift: cognitive trajectories appear shaped by intrinsic molecular set points rather than by chronological age, with expression of a motile ciliary program at the cerebrospinal fluid interface, rather than the abundance of the cells carrying it, emerging as a candidate correlate of resilience. This approach offers a generalizable strategy for dissecting functional heterogeneity from aging and identifying pathways for hypothesis-driven tests of resilience across the lifespan.

papers.title: Bats Could Learn Three-Dimensional Echolocation Using Echoacoustic Flow
papers.abstract: Echolocating bats can find prey and avoid obstacles in three dimensions using sound alone. They infer the direction of an echo from the way the emitter, the head and the outer ears filter sound, together described by the echolocation-related transfer functon(ERTF). This filter differs between species and is likely to change as the ears grow, so it has to be calibrated by experience. Barn owls and humans recalibrate auditory space after their ears are altered, instructed by vision in the owl and by a so far unidentified teacher in humans. How a bat flying in the dark could calibrate its ERTF is unknown. Here we show that a simulated bat-like agent can learn its ERTF in azimuth and elevation from its echoes and movements alone, using echoacoustic flow, without labeled echo directions or an external teacher such as vision. The agent encodes each call into a structured latent scene, moves it with a physics-based geometric warp and predicts the next echoes through a differentiable renderer. It learns its ERTF efficiently and relearns it quickly after its outer ears change. The results form a first functional model of how bats could learn spatial hearing and yield testable hypotheses for behavioral experiments.

papers.title: Biology Undergraduates Use of AI-Enabled Feedback to Revise Scientific Writing: Recipience and Barriers
papers.abstract: Background: Instructors and education researchers are increasingly developing feedback with the assistance of generative AI, which we refer to as AI-enabled feedback, yet we do not know whether established understandings of feedback uptake and effectiveness apply similarly in AI-mediated contexts. This makes the recipience of AI-enabled feedback a central concern to understanding how to best support students in developing their scientific writing skills. This study examined how two teams of undergraduate biology students used AI-enabled feedback to revise their scientific writing, and the extent to which their revisions addressed that feedback. The teams revised their research proposal drafts after receiving AI-enabled feedback developed by their instructor with the aid of a custom AI tool. Results: Our findings show that AI-enabled feedback prompted actionable revision across both teams. Each team addressed approximately half of the feedback comments, indicating comparable levels of uptake despite their differing approaches to revision. We observed that both teams were inconsistent in providing the additional information and reasoning requested in the feedback, and they struggled to address comments requiring self-evaluation. Taken together, we see that students often addressed the more easily actionable parts of AI-enabled feedback while omitting more demanding revisions. Conclusions: These findings provide behavioral evidence of how students used AI-enabled feedback to revise their scientific writing. The observed patterns suggest that the content of AI-enabled feedback supported meaningful revision, while limitations in students agency, strategies, and volition likely shaped their implementation of comments. Although the degree of uptake observed in this study is encouraging, it is unlikely that a single application of generative AI within the feedback process will resolve all the challenges associated with feedback uptake.
